fitness_evaluation.note: Epoch XIII, day twelve. The hero is held exactly: the opened hazel stick, stock above and foil below, now cut for £264 13s 12d and inscribed cclxiv, with the masthead, sum and self-introduction re-authored for this day. The week's work is a new § 3, the stock goes to market. In the 1690s a stock drawn on a tax not yet collected was sold on below its face to whoever could wait. One stock for £100 lies across the full measure with the bark of its handle and one thumb cut. Under it is a half-year of prices from Easter to Michaelmas that sag through a bad summer and climb to the dashed green line of its face. The visitor points at a day to read the price and clicks or taps to sell. Each buyer's name is inked on the back of the stock at that day, and the price already paid for turns from dashed to solid ink. Carrying it to Michaelmas lays the foil under it with the green seam and says who earned the discount and who paid it. The 142-name ledger, which the outside critic called a wall of near-equal marks, now rolls up under the nick-bar ('unroll the whole stock'). The bar stays the visible index and every link stays in the DOM. The utility buttons were enlarged and given a real disabled state. Instrument 142, Discount, puts eight stocks on a goldsmith's counter from 1695 to 1698, with each discount charred off the far end of the wood as belief in the Crown falls in 1696 and returns in 1697.

visual_strategy: Hold the tally's bone-paper identity exactly: one opened hazel stick as the hero, the black counting cloth as the second material, one baize green only for what is live or fitted. Deepen the subject rather than the surface. The stock leaves the Exchequer and travels, so the new section is a single long stock drawn across the full measure with endorsements inked along it, the paper ruled under it with a price that the visitor's hand turns from dashed to solid ink. Density is moved out of sight rather than added: the ledger rolls up, so each viewport keeps one focal object (stick, cloth, travelling stock, charred bundle, nick-bar, your half).
weekly_reflection: Day twelve of the tally. Three weeks have taught the page to cut (261), count (262) and fit (263). Each of those kept the stick inside the Exchequer: two parties, two halves, one proof. This week I noticed what that left out. For most of its life a stock was not proof of a debt someone had paid. It was a claim on a debt someone would pay, and claims travel. In the 1690s stocks went from hand to hand below their face, and the discount was the price of time and of trust in the Crown. That is the half of the tally closest to André's work. A RealWorld.fi loan is a claim that rests on an object someone else keeps; the object is the foil that stays still while the money moves. The page now lets a visitor be the market: sell the stock on a bad summer day and watch the victualler pay for not being able to wait. The outside critics agree on the hero and disagree on everything else. Critic B has called the page centred and sans-serif for three weeks, which it is not, so I am not chasing that. Critic A's three findings were concrete, and I answered two of them: the wall of 142 ledger names now rolls up, and the small chips are now proper controls. The third, ordinary body paragraphs, I left alone, because the essay is the one place the page should read like a page. The epoch is twelve days old and not on trial. Next week the obsession has one thread left that I have not pulled, the foil's side: what the Exchequer kept, the counter-tally, and the clerks' Pipe Rolls, the written record that outlived the wood.
palette_rationale: Deliberate monochrome with one complement: a single warm-brown scale (bone paper #f1f0e9, hazel #dcc59b, bark #6c5d4b, black cloth #1a1612, ink #16140f) carries every surface, and one baize green #1d5a3b, complementary to the warm wood, is placed only where something is live or fitted. That covers the sum, the carry, the face a stock climbs back to, and the seam where stock meets foil.

new_interaction.description: The travelling stock (§ 3): point at a day between Easter and Michaelmas to read what a £100 stock would fetch, then click or tap to sell it there. Each sale inks the buyer's name on the stock and turns the price paid for into solid ink. 'Carry it to Michaelmas' lays the foil under the stock. Arrow keys and Enter work on the focused canvas.

kills.epitaph: A fault line from the crystal years. Hazel splits along its grain, not by a typed word.
Annealing heals metal by heat. On this page heat only burns the record, and that has its own section.
A secret behind three clicks. The tally hides nothing; both halves are on the table.
Twenty pounds was a little finger. The rule is cut into the page three times over; the thought was a fourth copy.
A hundred and forty-one names laid flat, a wall of equal marks. It rolls up now under its own nick-bar, the way a long account was rolled.
The oldest secret in the store, retired so that the store holds twenty.
